reviewMethod.methodNotesMd: Reviewed the output contract, resource-level rubric, and fresh-review framework, then checked the SupplyDelivery structure report, resource-review context, deterministic aggregate, direct behavior findings, shared Resource/DomainResource behavior context, and the relevant R4/R6 package definitions. The deterministic aggregate was compared only after forming the resource-level conclusion. Shared Resource/DomainResource behavior findings were treated as context rather than scored SupplyDelivery findings.

r4Maturity.effectMd: SupplyDelivery was trial-use/FMM 1 in R4, so the standards-stability burden is weak. That softens the case for preserving the entire legacy resource, but it does not erase operational, audit, logistics, medication/device handoff, or inventory risk for implementers that actually stored or exchanged SupplyDelivery records.

overall.oneLineConclusion: R6 removes SupplyDelivery, making a resource-level migration or archival strategy unavoidable; low-cost maps and guidance still matter, but individual element preservation is not the main compatibility lever.

reasoning.thesisMd: The actual migration shape is resource identity loss. R4 defines `SupplyDelivery` as a concrete DomainResource for records of supplied items, while the inspected R6 package has no `StructureDefinition-SupplyDelivery.json`, no package-index entry, and no obvious same-resource successor. That means old instances fail at the top-level resource type before child elements, and generated R6 models, route inventories, search surfaces, and storage schemas cannot rely on a native SupplyDelivery class.
reasoning.migrationShapeMd: A real migration program is already unavoidable. R4 SupplyDelivery can represent medication, substance, or device delivery events with `basedOn`, self-referential `partOf`, status, type, patient, supplied item, occurrence, supplier, destination, and receiver. R6 `MedicationDispense` overlaps with medication delivery but is medication-specific and has its own mandatory `status`, `medication`, and `subject` semantics; `DeviceRequest` is a request rather than a completed delivery event. The result is not a single mechanical rename but classification, mapping policy, and sometimes archival or extension-based preservation.
reasoning.compatibilityLeverageMd: Because the resource itself is absent, preventing additional local element breaks has lower leverage than it would for a mostly stable resource. Preserving `status`, `type`, endpoint advertisements, or search parameters in isolation would not make an R4 SupplyDelivery instance a native R6 instance. The main base-compatible alternative would be retaining SupplyDelivery as a deprecated or legacy-compatible resource, but that is a whole-resource compatibility commitment with duplicate-model and support costs, not a cheap alias. Low-cost compatibility support is still valuable as migration guidance, ConceptMaps, StructureMaps, and explicit endpoint/search transition notes.
reasoning.lessBreakingAlternativesMd: The strongest less-breaking design would keep a deprecated SupplyDelivery resource, or a very explicit compatibility profile, while steering new implementations to domain-specific resources. That would preserve most R4 instances, but for an FMM 1 trial-use resource it has material cost: continued server/tool support, parallel generic and domain-specific representations, and ambiguity about when to use each path. More modest artifacts, especially status/type ConceptMaps and guidance for device/substance/generic deliveries, are standards-review-worthy because they reduce unsafe local mappings even though they do not remove the resource-identity break.
reasoning.behaviorImpactMd: The direct behavior findings reinforce the same resource-removal shape. The base CapabilityStatement no longer advertises a SupplyDelivery REST endpoint, and search parameters whose only base was SupplyDelivery disappear with the endpoint. These are real client/runtime migration concerns, but they are derivative of the missing resource rather than independent reasons to preserve old child elements. The 11 shared Resource/DomainResource behavior findings, such as Resource-level operations and core metadata search behavior, may affect cross-version infrastructure generally but were not scored as SupplyDelivery-specific because SupplyDelivery is not Resource or DomainResource.
reasoning.comparisonToDeterministicAggregateMd: I agree with the deterministic aggregate on the headline: major migration is `Yes`, the shape is `removed-or-replaced-resource`, and `migration-program-dominates` is the right compatibility-leverage conclusion. My independent calibration gives more weight to the weak R4 FMM/status than the raw Critical/High counts do: the removal is certainly breaking, but the case for reversing it is weaker than it would be for a mature or normative resource. The useful standards work is explicit migration support and optional legacy compatibility, not treating every derivative endpoint/search/terminology loss as separately avoidable.
reasoning.uncertaintyMd: Confidence is high for absence of the R6 resource in the inspected package and for the need for migration. Confidence is lower on production prevalence and official rationale because the local inputs did not include ballot discussion or official cross-version maps, and the R6 input is a ballot package.

findingConsiderations.title: SupplyDelivery resource is absent from the R6 core package
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This is the decisive finding. R4 instances with `resourceType` SupplyDelivery have no native R6 StructureDefinition, so validation, generated model classes, resource-specific endpoints, search, and storage all require migration or compatibility handling. The FMM 1/trial-use baseline makes the removal more tolerable than a mature resource removal, but it does not reduce the need for a migration program.

findingConsiderations.title: No single R6 successor preserves the SupplyDelivery event content model
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This finding explains why the migration is not merely changing the resource name. Medication deliveries may fit MedicationDispense in some cases, but device, substance, generic supply deliveries, event chains, SupplyRequest fulfillment links, destination, receiver, and participant semantics need policy decisions or preservation outside a single native R6 successor.

findingConsiderations.title: SupplyDelivery status and type terminology have no direct R6 continuation
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: The status/type issue is secondary to resource removal but still matters for safe migration. `entered-in-error` modifier semantics, `abandoned`, and the old medication/device type distinction should not be projected blindly into MedicationDispense or request-resource lifecycles. Official ConceptMaps or guidance would be relatively low-cost and reduce inconsistent local mappings.

findingConsiderations.title: Search parameters whose only R4 bases were removed resources disappear from the R6 search surface
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This is directly in scope because SupplyDelivery is among the affected resources. It matters for clients that query SupplyDelivery routes, but it is derivative: without a native SupplyDelivery endpoint or successor mapping, preserving the old search parameters alone would not solve the core migration.

findingConsiderations.title: The full base CapabilityStatement no longer advertises many R4 resource REST endpoints
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: The missing SupplyDelivery REST endpoint is a real discoverability and generated-client concern. However, endpoint preservation would effectively require supporting the removed resource or a compatibility alias, so this finding follows from the resource-identity decision rather than creating a separate low-cost break to avoid.

findingConsiderations.title: Required input parameter renamed from `input` to `resource`
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This Resource-level operation change can affect generic cross-version conversion tooling, including tooling that might be used during SupplyDelivery migration. Per the resource-review rules, it is shared Resource behavior and is not counted as a SupplyDelivery-specific behavior finding.

findingConsiderations.title: Core special/profile search parameters changed type metadata for _content, _text, _query, and _profile
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This shared search-metadata issue may affect infrastructure around all resources, but it is not specific to SupplyDelivery and does not change the resource-level conclusion that SupplyDelivery migration is dominated by resource removal.

recommendedNextActions.actionMd: Publish explicit SupplyDelivery migration guidance that classifies records by supplied item domain and workflow context, identifies when MedicationDispense is appropriate, and defines how to preserve device, substance, generic supply, `partOf`, destination, receiver, provenance, and audit information when no native R6 target is clean.

Provide official status/type mapping tables or ConceptMaps, including policy notes for `entered-in-error`, `abandoned`, omitted status, and the old medication/device type distinction, so implementations do not create incompatible local mappings.

Document endpoint and search migration expectations for retired SupplyDelivery routes, including whether legacy aliases are implementation-specific compatibility features and how old queries should be rewritten after the resource mapping is chosen.

If evidence of significant production dependence emerges, consider a deprecated legacy SupplyDelivery compatibility resource or profile; absent that evidence, the FMM 1/trial-use status makes full resource retention a lower-priority compatibility option.

caveats: The local R6 ballot package proves absence of a native SupplyDelivery resource, but it does not include the standards rationale for removal.
Production prevalence of R4 SupplyDelivery use was not established by the supplied local inputs.
Shared Resource and DomainResource behavior findings were reviewed only as context, not as SupplyDelivery-specific drivers.
Candidate target-resource analysis was limited to relevant local R6 artifacts and did not attempt a full design review of every possible extension or implementation guide.
